Paper 1 – Question 1. Read Source D.

Source D
"No country decides alone any more. The dollar, the semiconductor supply chain and the undersea cables are the real architecture of power."
— Lecture on international political economy, 2023 (adapted)

Identify three elements of the "architecture of power" listed in Source D. [3]

items.stem:
Paper 1 – Question 2. Read Source D.

Source D
"The textbooks tell the story of treaties signed by men in grand halls. They do not tell of the women who kept the villages alive during the war, or of those who negotiated local ceasefires."
— Women peacebuilders' network, 2019 (adapted)

Explain, with reference to Source D, a feminist critique of traditional international relations. [4]
items.answer: Traditional accounts focus on elite male actors and formal diplomacy; feminist approaches ask "where are the women?" and highlight women's roles in survival and peacebuilding.
items.markingKey: Traditional accounts focus on elite male actors and formal diplomacy; feminist approaches ask "where are the women?" and highlight women's roles in survival and peacebuilding. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source; 1–2 marks: limited explanation or mainly quotation/description without explanation.

items.answer: Similarities: both see economic tools as central to power; both point to infrastructure as a basis of influence. Differences: Source C focuses on bilateral relationships and local doubts; Source D on global structures; C stresses legitimacy on the ground; D stresses material control.
items.markingKey: Similarities: both see economic tools as central to power; both point to infrastructure as a basis of influence. items.stem: Paper 2 – To what extent do you agree that feminist perspectives have changed how global institutions understand security? Support your answer with specific contemporary case studies. [15]

items.stem: Paper 2 – "The individual is the least important level of analysis in global politics." Discuss, with reference to at least one theoretical perspective and two real-world examples. [15]

items.stem: Paper 2 – Evaluate the claim that the world is returning to bipolarity between the United States and China. In your answer, refer to at least two contrasting examples. [15]
items.answer: US–China rivalry is the central axis, but deep interdependence and autonomous middle powers make the system more complex than Cold War bipolarity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: US and China have far larger economies and military budgets than others; competition in tech, trade and the Indo-Pacific. Arguments against: Russia, India and the EU remain significant; deep economic interdependence unlike the Cold War; many states refuse to choose sides. Possible judgement: US–China rivalry is the central axis, but deep interdependence and autonomous middle powers make the system more complex than Cold War bipolarity. Markbands (15): 13–15 – sharply focused on the demands of the question; detailed, accurate knowledge of relevant concepts, theories and specific contemporary examples; well-developed, balanced counter-claims; a clear, consistent and well-supported conclusion. 10–12 – focused and well structured; relevant, accurate knowledge and examples; counter-claims addressed; reasoned conclusion. 7–9 – mostly focused; relevant knowledge with some examples; some counter-claims; conclusion stated. 4–6 – some understanding of the demands; limited or general knowledge, mainly descriptive; little evaluation. 1–3 – little understanding; minimal relevant knowledge; no evaluation. 0 – does not reach the standard of band 1.

items.stem:
Paper 3 – Question 1. Read the stimulus.

Stimulus: Rwanda's 2003 constitution set a 30% minimum quota for women in decision-making bodies; women now hold over 60% of seats in the lower house.

With reference to the stimulus, explain one way in which Rwanda and women's representation illustrates implementation of CEDAW principles. [4]
items.answer: constitutional measures turned treaty commitments into strong outcomes for political representation
items.markingKey: constitutional measures turned treaty commitments into strong outcomes for political representation. 1 mark for identifying a relevant feature from the stimulus; up to 3 further marks for explaining clearly how it links to the concept.

items.stem:
Paper 3 – Question 2. Read the stimulus.

Stimulus: The EU, US and allies froze Russian central bank assets, cut some banks from SWIFT and banned many imports and exports.

Using the stimulus and one other example you have studied, analyse the roles of the actors involved in Western sanctions on Russia after February 2022 in relation to hard economic power. [9]
items.answer: sanctions are coercive tools to raise the cost of the invasion, but Russia's continued war shows the limits of hard power. A second, contrasting example is analysed alongside the stimulus.
items.markingKey: Stimulus: sanctions are coercive tools to raise the cost of the invasion, but Russia's continued war shows the limits of hard power. Own example must be specific and explicitly compared. 7–9: sustained analysis of actors and the concept, using both stimulus and own example; 4–6: some analysis, uneven use of the stimulus or example; 1–3: mostly descriptive.

items.stem:
Paper 3 – Question 3. Read the stimulus.

Stimulus: After a decade of liberalisation, privatisation and a currency peg, Argentina defaulted on about $95 billion of debt in 2001, causing a deep recession and political turmoil.

"The Beijing Consensus offers a better model of development for the Global South than the Washington Consensus." With reference to the stimulus and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree with this statement? [15]
items.answer: China's experience offers lessons on state capacity and gradualism, but it is not easily replicated, and no single model fits all.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: China's growth and poverty reduction; infrastructure focus; no governance conditions. Arguments against: depends on China's specific conditions; authoritarian costs; debt from BRI loans. Possible judgement: China's experience offers lessons on state capacity and gradualism, but it is not easily replicated, and no single model fits all. The stimulus should be used as evidence, not merely summarised.
